items.stem: A course grade is 0.5 × exam + 0.3 × project + 0.2 × quiz. Which operation from this panel is that?

options.text: A dot product: multiply each pair of numbers and add them.
options.feedback: The scores and the weights are two vectors. Pairing them, multiplying and adding gives one number.

options.text: A slope: how fast the grade changes with a score.
options.feedback: A slope would tell you how much the grade changes when one score changes. This formula gives the grade itself.

options.text: A distribution: outcomes with probabilities that add to 1.
options.feedback: The weights do add to 1 here, but a distribution describes the chance of outcomes. These weights describe how much each score counts.

options.text: A loss: how wrong a prediction is, compared with the truth.
options.feedback: A loss compares a prediction with the truth. This formula involves no prediction.

items.stem: Vector a points right. Vector b points straight up, at a right angle to a. What is a · b?

options.feedback: Vector b has no part along a, so the two vectors share nothing.
A large positive number needs the arrows to point the same way.
A negative number needs the arrows to point apart, at more than a right angle.

options.text: It depends on how long b is.
options.feedback: Length changes the size of the dot product when the arrows are partly aligned. At a right angle the answer is zero for any length.

items.stem: On the loss curve, the slope at your current weight is +3. To make the model less wrong, which way should you move the weight?

options.feedback: A positive slope means the curve rises as you go right. Moving the opposite way from the slope lowers the loss.
This follows the slope, so the loss would rise. Training moves against the slope.
You stop only where the slope is zero. A slope of +3 means the loss can still go down.

options.text: It depends on the learning rate.
options.feedback: The learning rate sets how far you move. The direction comes from the sign of the slope.

items.stem: A model reports next-word probabilities of 0.5, 0.3 and 0.4 for three words and nothing for any others. What is wrong?

options.text: They add up to 1.2. A distribution must add up to 1.
options.feedback: The probabilities of all possible outcomes together cover everything that can happen, so they must add up to 1, or 100%.

options.text: Nothing. Each number is between 0 and 1.
options.feedback: Each number is valid alone. The whole set must also add up to 1.

options.text: The numbers are too large for probabilities.
options.feedback: A single word can have a large probability. The problem is the total.

options.text: A model can only give two probabilities at a time.
options.feedback: A model gives a probability for every word it can choose.
